narrative:
The model predicted a 56% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability tipped above 50%, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

The three factors that mattered most in this decision were, in order of importance, your undergraduate GPA, your LSAT score, and your third-year law school grades. Your undergraduate GPA of 2.80 was the strongest influence and pushed the prediction toward failure; it sits noticeably below the 3.23 average of students who were accepted. This single factor carried more weight than any other in the model’s reasoning.

Your LSAT score of 37 worked in the opposite direction. It is almost exactly at the average of accepted students and therefore pulled the prediction slightly toward passing. However, this positive effect was not large enough to overcome the downward pressure from your GPA.

Your third-year grades, which placed you in the fifth decile, added a modest additional push toward failure. While this was weaker than the first two factors, it still reinforced the overall outlook.

Taken together, these academic signals led the model to conclude you were more likely than not to struggle with the bar exam. To improve your chances on a future application, focus on strengthening your academic record—whether by raising your grades in remaining law school courses, gaining targeted bar-prep experience, or demonstrating strong performance on practice exams—so the next prediction falls comfortably below the 50% threshold.
